user.name: Charley Dunkel
user.backstory: Charley's weather app works now, and it's saved on GitHub. Next up: a dark mode. But Charley doesn't want to risk breaking the version that already works.

cards.title: What is a branch?
body: A branch is a separate line of snapshots. Think of it as a second save slot in a game: you can try something risky there, and your main save stays safe. Every project starts with one branch, called `main`.

cards.title: Make a branch and move onto it
body: `git switch -c add-dark-mode` creates a new branch called `add-dark-mode` and moves you onto it. The `-c` means "create." From now on, new snapshots go on this branch, and `main` isn't touched.
Older tutorials use `git checkout -b add-dark-mode`, which does the same thing.

cards.title: See your branches
body: `git branch` lists all your branches. The one with a `*` next to it is the branch you're on right now.

questions.prompt: Why would Charley make a branch for dark mode?
options: To delete old snapshots
To upload the project to GitHub
To try changes without affecting `main`
questions.wrongFeedback: A branch is like a second save slot: Charley can experiment there while `main` stays safe.

questions.prompt: When you run `git branch`, what does the `*` mean?
options: That's the branch you're on right now
That's the newest branch
That branch has an error
questions.wrongFeedback: The `*` marks the branch you're currently on.

user.name: Charley Dunkel
user.backstory: Charley finished dark mode on the `add-dark-mode` branch and tested it. It works. Now it's time to merge it into `main`, the real version of the app, using GitHub.

cards.title: Merging happens on GitHub
body: Merging brings the snapshots from one branch into another, like copying the progress from your experimental save slot into your main save. Most teams don't merge in the terminal. They merge on GitHub with a pull request: a page that says "here are my changes, please merge them," so teammates can look first.

cards.title: Step 1: upload your branch
body: GitHub can only merge what it can see, so first push your branch:
cards.footer: It's the same push from Unit 1, just with your branch's name instead of `main`. GitHub will then offer a Compare & pull request button.

cards.title: Step 2: set base and compare
body: When you open a pull request, GitHub asks for two branches:
bullets: base: the branch you're merging into (usually `main`)
compare: the branch with your changes
cards.footer: The arrow shows the direction: changes flow from compare into base.

cards.title: Step 3: merge, then bring it home
body: Click Merge pull request, then Confirm merge. Now `main` on GitHub has dark mode, but your laptop doesn't yet. Switch to `main` and run `git pull` to download it.
(If both branches changed the same lines, GitHub warns you about a conflict before you can merge.)

questions.prompt: Charley opens a pull request on GitHub. Which setup merges dark mode into `main`?
options: `base: add-dark-mode  <--  compare: main`
`base: main  <--  compare: add-dark-mode`
`base: main  <--  compare: main`
questions.wrongFeedback: Base is where the changes go (`main`). Compare is the branch with the changes (`add-dark-mode`).

options: Yes, it updates automatically
No, Charley has to merge again in the terminal
No, Charley needs to download it with `git pull`

user.name: Jackson Stark
user.welcomeTitle: Jackson's back, and joining a team!
user.backstory: Charley's weather app is getting popular, and Jackson wants to help by adding a 5-day forecast. Charley invited Jackson to the project on GitHub. Time to work together.

cards.title: How teams share one project
body: A team shares one repo on GitHub. Each person works on their own branch, and changes reach `main` through pull requests, just like Charley did in the last lesson. Charley added Jackson as a collaborator in the repo's settings, so Jackson is allowed to push to it.

cards.title: Get your own copy with `git clone`
body: `git clone <url>` downloads the whole project, with its full history, into a new folder on your laptop. You only clone once. Copy the URL from GitHub, like Lily did in Unit 1.
Then move into the new folder with `cd weather-app`, and make your own branch, just like in Lesson 1.

cards.title: Review before you merge
body: When a teammate opens a pull request, you review it on GitHub. Read the changes in the Files changed tab, leave comments, then choose Approve or Request changes. Reviews catch bugs before they reach `main`.

cards.title: Stay up to date
body: Your teammates keep merging things into `main`. Before you start something new, switch to `main` and run `git pull`, so you're building on the latest version and not an old one.

questions.prompt: Download Charley's project to Jackson's laptop. Use the Copy button on the profile card.
You're in the project folder. Create a branch called `add-forecast` and switch to it.
Jackson finished the forecast and opened a pull request. While reviewing it, Charley spots a bug. What should Charley do?
options: Leave a review and choose "Request changes"
Merge it anyway and fix the bug later
Delete Jackson's branch
questions.wrongFeedback: That's what reviews are for: Charley chooses "Request changes" so Jackson can fix the bug before it reaches `main`.

questions.prompt: Jackson fixed the bug, and Charley merged the pull request. Why should Jackson run `git pull` on `main` before starting something new?
options: To upload Jackson's work to GitHub
To delete old branches
To get everything the team merged, so new work starts from the latest version
questions.wrongFeedback: `git pull` downloads what teammates merged, so Jackson builds on the newest `main`. Uploading is `git push`.

user.name: Lily Lurvey
user.backstory: Lily's portfolio has been live on GitHub since Unit 1. But today two things went wrong: an edit Lily hasn't saved yet broke the home page, and a commit Lily already pushed broke the contact form. Time to undo both.

cards.title: Everyone makes mistakes
body: Undoing mistakes is one of the best things about Git. Which tool you use depends on one question: have you committed yet?

cards.title: `git restore`: throw away changes you haven't committed
body: `git restore index.html` puts the file back the way it was in your last snapshot.
Careful: those changes are gone for good, because Git never saved them. If it worked, Git prints nothing.

cards.title: Find the commit with `git log`
body: `git log --oneline` lists your snapshots, newest first, one per line. HEAD means the snapshot you're on right now, which is usually the newest one.

cards.title: `git revert`: undo a commit safely
body: `git revert HEAD` makes a new snapshot that undoes the newest one. The broken commit stays in the history, but its changes are reversed. That's safe even after you've pushed, because your teammates' history doesn't get rewritten. Then `git push` to share the fix.
(In a real terminal, Git opens a text editor for the message. Just save and close it, or add `--no-edit` to skip it.)

questions.prompt: Lily changed `index.html` and broke the home page, but hasn't committed yet. What will `git restore index.html` do?
options: Delete `index.html`
Undo Lily's last commit
Throw away the uncommitted changes and go back to the last snapshot
questions.wrongFeedback: `git restore` throws away changes you haven't committed. The file goes back to the last snapshot.

questions.prompt: Throw away Lily's broken changes to `index.html`.
The broken "Add contact form" commit is already on GitHub. Why should Lily use `git revert`?
options: It deletes the commit so nobody ever sees it
It adds a new snapshot that undoes the change, without rewriting history
It brings back changes Lily never committed
questions.wrongFeedback: `git revert` doesn't delete anything. It adds a new snapshot that reverses the bad one, which is safe for commits already on GitHub.
